Note that Rust is not a theorem prover and Rust programs are usually not formally verified (there are some extensions like Creusot to verify Rust programs, but they are incomplete and a work in progress)

Compiler bugs are, like, just logic bugs. There's a project to eliminate compiler bugs that cause unsoundness, project zero [0] but, still, without formally verifying the implementation, there is nothing really guaranteeing there's no such bugs left.

(note: unsoundness in this context means having safe code cause UB due to a compiler bug; the fix is usually to make the compiler reject the code with a compiler error)

To make matters worse, Rust still doesn't have a spec, and there is not even a tight definition of what are the rules of unsafe code - that is, what rules you must follow so that you unsafe code doesn't trigger UB. Discussions around this are done mainly in issues of the unsafe code guidelines repo [1]

That takes me back to an early 1980s incident where I was criticized for an early computer-generated proof. This was when I was building a program verifier at an aerospace company. We had the first SAT solver, the Oppen-Nelson simplifier, and the first constructive theorem prover, the Boyer-Moore prover.[1] I wanted to show that the four axioms of arrays, which the simplifier assumed to be true, were valid in Boyer-Moore theory.

Boyer and Moore had warned me of the soundness risks of adding axioms to their prover. So I tried to prove them from basic Boyer-Moore theory, which is close to the Peano axioms. Boyer-Moore theory is LISP-like in form. You start with (ZERO) and (ADD1 X). So two is represented as (ADD1 (ADD1 (ZERO))). It's all lists of tuples at the bottom.

Equality is strict. (EQUAL A B) is true only if the representations of both A and B are identical. This creates a problem. An array can be represented as a list of (index, value), but for EQUAL to work, the list has to be ordered by subscript and each subscript unique. So storing into an array is represented as insertion into an ordered list. That generates a lot of special cases.

Accessing an array is a linear list search by recursion:

    (DEFN selecta (A I)
        (IF (EQUAL (array-elt-subscript A) I) 
            (array-elt-value A) 
            (IF (EQUAL (array-prev A) (empty-array)) 
                (UNDEFINED)
                (selecta (array-prev A) I))))
That's around line 3276 in [2]. The other definitions of array operations are similarly simple. Then we get to proving the classic four axioms of arrays.

Around 3000 lines later, the classic four "axioms" of arrays have been proved. Much grinding through special cases. It's a neat result, but bulky.

So I submitted a paper to JACM. Reviewer comments included "I hate to see something this complicated at the foundations of computer science", and just "This is unnecessary." People were really upset by all that case analysis.

The theoretical problem was that I didn't have set theory. I could have built up set theory first, before array theory, then used set theory to prove array theory. That probably would have made mathematicians happier. Or not. Set theory is traditionally axiomatic, but it can be built up from constructive Boyer-Moore tuple theory if desired.

I didn't argue with the reviewers. I probably could have found a more elegant path to this result, by creating intermediate lemmas, rather than letting the prover grind through the cases on automatic. But I wasn't going for a PhD. I had real work to do at an aerospace company.

So, I've been beaten on by the academic community for a bulky machine proof. Today, nobody would be bothered by this approach. It's only a few thousand lines, and a human can follow it. You can be too early.

(You can still run this prover today. I converted it to GNU Common LISP a decade ago. It takes about one second on a modern machine to go from the Peano-like axioms to array theory. It took 45 minutes on the VAX 11/780 I was using back in the early 1980s.)
